title: Supraclavicular / Submental Island Pedicled Flaps
linked_topic: Reconstruction Selection After Head & Neck Ablation
source_label: Pasha 6e regional flap section, with Cummings 7e reconstruction principles
indications: Thin, pliable, single-stage fasciocutaneous island flaps that serve as alternatives to free tissue transfer in patients who are poor free-flap candidates, have a vessel-depleted neck, or need a modest defect closed quickly. The supraclavicular artery island flap (transverse cervical system) suits lateral face, parotid, neck skin, pharyngeal and oral defects and tracheostoma or pharyngocutaneous fistula repair. The submental island flap (facial artery system) suits oral cavity, lower face and lip defects. The submental flap is avoided when level I nodes are clinically involved, and the supraclavicular flap when the transverse cervical vessels have been taken or level V radiated heavily without a Doppler signal.
setup: Supine with shoulder roll and head turned away; prep the neck, shoulder and deltoid (supraclavicular) or entire submandibular and submental region (submental)
Handheld Doppler at the table; map and mark the pedicle and the distal-most signal before incision
Pinch test for paddle width so the donor site closes primarily (about 6 to 8 cm for supraclavicular, 5 to 7 cm for submental)
Bipolar, fine scissors, vessel clips, loupes; plan neck dissection incisions so they do not cut the pedicle
Agree the sequence with the ablative team: in a neck dissection, preserve the facial artery and vein or the transverse cervical vessels deliberately
landmarks: Supraclavicular triangle: posterior border of SCM, external jugular vein, and middle third of the clavicle
Transverse cervical artery and supraclavicular branch exiting about 2 to 3 cm above the clavicle behind the SCM
Deltoid fascia and acromion as the distal axis of the supraclavicular paddle
Facial artery and vein at the inferior border of the mandible and the submental branch running along the mylohyoid
Anterior belly of digastric, often included with the submental pedicle
Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve over the facial vessels
danger: Extending the supraclavicular paddle more than about 5 cm beyond the last Doppler signal invites distal necrosis
Twisting or tunnel compression of a short pedicle
Marginal mandibular nerve injury while dissecting the facial vessels
Transferring occult level IA/IB nodal disease into the oral cavity with a submental flap
Thin venous drainage of the submental flap: the submental vein may join the facial vein low or variably
Donor closure under tension, which can choke the pedicle
steps: Choose the flap

Match defect size, location and arc of rotation. The supraclavicular flap pivots near the clavicle and reaches the lateral face, parotid bed, pharynx and neck. The submental flap pivots at the facial vessels near the mandible and reaches the oral cavity, lip and lower face. Confirm the vessels are intact on imaging, operative notes and Doppler.
Mark the supraclavicular flap

Locate the transverse cervical/supraclavicular pulse in the triangle formed by the SCM, external jugular vein and clavicle. Draw the axis from this point toward the acromion and over the deltoid. Design an ellipse of the needed length centered on the axis, keeping the distal tip within about 5 cm of the last audible signal.
Raise supraclavicular distal to proximal

Incise the distal paddle down through the deltoid fascia and elevate in the subfascial plane toward the clavicle. Including the fascia protects the axial vessels running on its deep surface. Hemostasis with bipolar only near the pedicle. Slow down once over the clavicle and trapezius border.
Isolate the supraclavicular pedicle

Near the triangle, either de-epithelialize the proximal skin or skeletonize a fascial pedicle to create an island. Visualize the pedicle by transillumination or Doppler rather than dissecting it bare. Stop elevation once the arc reaches the defect without tension; further dissection near the vessel origin adds risk with little reach.
Transfer and close the shoulder

Tunnel under a generous cervical skin bridge or open the bridge, checking for twist and compression. Inset in layers with the paddle edges bleeding. Close the shoulder donor primarily after undermining; skin graft any segment that will not close without tension. Place a drain in the donor bed.
Mark the submental flap

With the head extended, outline an ellipse in the submental crease below the mandibular border, sized by pinch test so the neck still closes. Doppler the submental artery near its origin from the facial artery, just below the mandible and medial to the submandibular gland.
Expose the facial vessels

Incise the inferior margin first and raise subplatysmal flaps. Find the facial artery and vein at the lower mandibular border, identify and protect the marginal mandibular nerve above them, and trace the submental branch medially along the mylohyoid. Preserve the facial vein and check where the submental vein drains.
Raise the submental island

Elevate the paddle from the contralateral side toward the pedicle, deep to platysma. Include the ipsilateral anterior belly of digastric and a cuff of mylohyoid fascia when the artery runs deep to the digastric, which protects its perforators. Clip mylohyoid and gland branches; separate the submandibular gland off the pedicle.
Lengthen the submental pedicle

Dissect the facial artery and vein proximally toward the external carotid and internal jugular if more reach is needed. Divide the distal facial vessels above the submental take-off for a reverse-flow design to the midface only when retrograde flow is confirmed. Avoid stripping adventitia during this dissection.
Clear level I with oncologic intent

When the flap is used for cancer, examine and clear level IA and IB nodes off the pedicle while leaving the vessels intact. Frozen section or abandonment of the flap is preferable to carrying suspicious nodes into the defect. Send any tissue removed from the pedicle as part of the neck specimen.
Transfer the submental flap

Pass the island through a tunnel beneath the mandible or through the floor-of-mouth defect into the oral cavity, keeping the pedicle free of kinks and away from bone edges. Inset with absorbable sutures in a watertight fashion to seal the oral cavity from the neck.
Close and check perfusion

Close the submental donor primarily over a drain, which also produces a mild neck-lift effect. Before leaving the room, check both flaps for color, capillary refill and bright edge bleeding. Position tracheostomy ties and dressings so they do not cross either pedicle.
exit_check: Island pink with brisk capillary refill and bright edge bleeding
Pedicle untwisted, no tunnel compression, no tight ties or dressings across it
Donor sites closed without tension or grafted; drains in place
postop: Hourly flap checks initially, using color, capillary refill, temperature and pinprick if needed
Head positioning that avoids rotation compressing the pedicle
Drains until output falls; watch for neck or shoulder hematoma
Shoulder range-of-motion exercises after supraclavicular harvest
Swallow and diet progression per defect after intraoral inset

early: Distal tip necrosis or partial paddle loss
Hematoma or seroma at the donor site
Wound dehiscence at the shoulder donor
late: Hair growth on an intraoral submental paddle in men
Regional recurrence in the flap territory from inadequate level I clearance

attending_followup: What vessel supplies the supraclavicular artery island flap and where is it found?

The supraclavicular artery, a branch of the transverse cervical artery (usually from the thyrocervical trunk). It is located in the triangle bounded by the posterior border of the SCM, the external jugular vein and the clavicle, roughly 2 to 3 cm above the clavicle, and runs toward the acromion over the deltoid.
Why is the deltoid fascia included in the supraclavicular flap?

The axial vessels run along the deep surface of the fascia. Subfascial elevation keeps them in the flap, protecting perfusion of the distal paddle. Leaving the fascia behind converts the distal part into a random flap.
What is the main oncologic concern with the submental island flap?

Level I lymph nodes lie along the submental pedicle. In node-positive oral cancer, transferring the flap can carry metastatic disease into the reconstruction. Careful level I clearance around the pedicle is mandatory, and many avoid the flap when level I is clinically involved.
What limits the reach of each flap and how can it be extended?

Pedicle length and pivot point. The supraclavicular flap is limited by its pivot near the clavicle; a longer paddle extends reach but distal reliability falls beyond the Doppler signal. The submental pedicle can be extended by dissecting the facial vessels to their origin or by a reverse-flow design for midface defects.
Why choose a regional island flap over a free flap?

Single-stage, shorter operation, no microvascular anastomosis, thin pliable tissue with good color match, and reliable in patients with significant comorbidity or a vessel-depleted neck. The trade-offs are limited size and reach and dependence on vessels that a prior neck dissection may have sacrificed.
